A commission was established to investigate the loss of the Royal Charter steam clipper, holding its meetings in Liverpool starting on February 6, 1860. The inquiry was led by Mr. Tremenheere and assisted by Captains Gray and Harris from the Board of Trade.

The Royal Charter was a 2,719-ton register ship built in 1855 at Sandycroft on the Clyde. Under the command of Captain John Taylor, who had been with the vessel since its first voyage, the ship departed Melbourne on August 26, 1859. On board were 112 crew members, 388 passengers, and a general cargo that included 39 boxes containing 79,000 ounces of gold destined for banks in London.

Following a fifty-nine-day journey characterized by heavy westerly winds, the ship rounded the Mull of Galloway on the morning of October 25 and took two pilots on board at Point Lynas. By 10:00 p.m. that evening, the wind had shifted to the northeast and reached hurricane force. Despite the ship's 200 nominal horsepower engines being worked to their full capacity, the vessel drifted stern-first toward the coast of Anglesey. At 1:30 a.m. on October 26, the ship struck rocks located half a mile east of Moelfre.

Rescue efforts began with the launch of a boat that was immediately destroyed against the side of the ship. However, a raft built by the carpenter, Peter Gibson, successfully carried the purser and twenty men to shore. Additionally, nineteen more people were saved using a buoy line rigged by the mate, Joseph Rodgers. Out of the 500 people on board, only 41 survived.

Almost all the gold sank with the ship, except for one box containing 1,640 ounces, which was found on the beach at Moelfre in November by a local man named Robert Williams.

The commission concluded that the ship was well-equipped and seaworthy. They found that when the wind shifted, the pilots had advised the ship to head out to sea, but Captain Taylor ignored this advice and decided to anchor in Moelfre roads instead. As a result of the disaster, the commission recommended the creation of a lifeboat station at Moelfre and a storm signal station at Point Lynas; the Marine Board provided both within two years.
